title: Classes and properties
bridge: C# classes have fields, constructors and methods like Java, plus **properties**: `public int Health { get; private set; }` reads like a field but controls who can change it.

exercises.title: An enemy
exercises.prompt: Make class Enemy with a read-only Name, Health with a private setter, a constructor Enemy(string name, int health), TakeDamage(int amount) (never below 0; negative amounts throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException), Heal(int amount) (never above the starting health), IsDead, and ToString() like "Goblin (18 HP)".

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var e = new Enemy("Goblin", 30); e.TakeDamage(12); return e.ToString() + " " + e.IsDead; }))()
((Func<string>)(() => { var e = new Enemy("Orc", 20); e.TakeDamage(50); e.Heal(5); return e.Health + " " + e.IsDead; }))()
((Func<string>)(() => { var e = new Enemy("Orc", 20); e.TakeDamage(5); e.Heal(100); return e.Health.ToString(); }))()
tests.hint_if_fail: Heal never goes above the starting health: keep it in a field.

tests.why: Health should have a private setter.

hints: public int Health { get; private set; }  and a private readonly int maxHealth;

quiz.q: public int Health { get; private set; } means…
choices: anyone can read it, only the class can change it

quiz.q: Why not a public field for Health?
choices: Other code could set it to -50; the class can't protect its rules

quiz.q: How is a Unity script shaped?
choices: A class with state (fields) and methods the engine calls

explain: Explain classes and properties to someone who has never programmed, in your own words, with an example you make up.
